summary: Delivery research has questioned the defect-catching value of formal change approval for years; agent pipelines make the cost side unbearable. The substitution only holds where the gates are real, where completion is verifiable without a human reading the diff, and where the non-defect functions of review are re-homed.

points.text: First-hand case study, Agent Studio, July to August 2026: zero pull requests are opened for the system's own development. The run agent does no git (ADR-0052); the platform commits the run, publishes a fenced delivery ref, runs a fail-closed build-and-test gate and named review aspects (Pass, Concerns, Block), integrates a green delivery into develop before the card reaches Human Review, and recomputes the card's integration state from git ancestry of its attributed commits. A card cannot reach Completed while that state is not integrated unless an operator override is set explicitly and recorded. Qualitative single-organization evidence; no defect-escape rate is claimed.

The same system publishes its own loop costs. For the last 30 days on 2026-08-23 (416 tasks) it counts 5,842 lane moves, 1,187 backwards; operator and escalation requeues leak the most time (95 and 52 days of rework in total), while build/test gate failures and quality-loop reopens recover in minutes. The gate layer is fast; the expensive loops end at a human.

Integration, acceptance, release and stable freeze are kept as four separate events: a task may be on develop while its card is still in review, and a release shows exactly which reviewed and unreviewed work is in the stream. That separation is what makes integrate-before-review safe to read; a single merged flag would hide it.

DORA finds no evidence that a more formal, external review process is associated with lower change fail rates, and reports that heavyweight approval slows delivery into larger, riskier batches. That weakens the assumption that removing a human approval step must cost stability.

The Google study of nine million reviewed changes describes modern code review as fast, lightweight and usually single-reviewer, with its dominant value in education, ownership and norm-keeping rather than in finding defects. Naming those functions is what makes the substitution honest: they must move somewhere, they do not disappear with the pull request.

SSDF PW.7 treats human code review and tool-based code analysis as selectable and combinable controls, and PW.7.2 requires that discovered issues be recorded and triaged in the team's workflow. An automated path can satisfy the practice if its standard is documented and its findings are tracked, which is exactly what a structured verdict and a recorded override provide.

The claim is scoped to the review gate, not to version control hygiene. Branch, merge and a durable trail all remain; what is removed is the human diff-reading step as the mandatory condition for integration.
